title: Tamil Cinema's 'Screenplay King' K Bhagyaraj Dies at 73 — and an Entire Industry Falls Silent
excerpt: Rajinikanth wept, Kamal Haasan mourned losing two Rajans in one month, and CM Vijay announced state honours for the man whose stories became Bollywood's biggest remakes
body:
The phone calls started before dawn on Saturday. By mid-morning, K Bhagyaraj — the man Tamil cinema simply called *the Screenplay King* — was gone. A massive cardiac arrest at his Chennai home ended a fifty-year career that shaped not just one film industry but two, quietly handing Bollywood some of its most beloved hits while the Hindi audience rarely learned his name.

He was 73. He had been dancing at a wedding in Goa two days earlier.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=ZhZ0VheFkek

The Genius Behind Your Favourite Hindi Films

Here is the thing most Bollywood fans don't know: some of the biggest Hindi hits of the '80s and '90s were K Bhagyaraj originals. Woh Saat Din, Beta, Mr. Bechara, Raja Babu, Andaz — all remakes of his Tamil films. His 1984 masterpiece *Oru Kaithiyin Diary* with Kamal Haasan provided the narrative blueprint that, decades later, became the skeleton for Shah Rukh Khan's ₹1,100-crore juggernaut Jawan. He never chased credit. He just kept writing.

> "K Bhagyaraj's Rajan — the man I was introduced to 50 years ago — is no more today. Tamil-speaking cinema has lost two Rajas within the same month." — Kamal Haasan

> "Tamil-speaking cinema has lost two Rajas within the same month." — Kamal Haasan**

That line cuts deep."**

That line cuts deep. Bhagyaraj's mentor, the legendary Bharathiraja, passed away earlier this month. Two architects of modern Tamil cinema, gone within weeks of each other. An era doesn't just end — it collapses.

Rajinikanth Broke Down

Superstar Rajinikanth arrived at Bhagyaraj's home in Chennai and immediately embraced his son, actor Shanthanu Bhagyaraj, who was visibly shattered. The footage went viral within minutes — Rajinikanth, a man who has played invincible on screen for four decades, undone by grief. He held Shanthanu for a long time before turning to console Bhagyaraj's wife, Poornima, a former actress herself.

![Chennai — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/32/Chennai_Central.jpg)

Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay — the actor-turned-politician who once dreamed of making films with Bhagyaraj — visited the home personally, announced full state honours, and called it "an irreplaceable loss." Chiranjeevi, Venkatesh Daggubati, R Madhavan, and Radhikaa Sarathkumar all followed with their own tributes. Venkatesh, who starred in Telugu remakes of Bhagyaraj's films like *Sundarakanda* and *Abbaigaru*, called his storytelling "timeless."

Five Decades of Brilliance

Born Krishnaswamy Bhagyaraj in Tamil Nadu's Erode district, he apprenticed under Bharathiraja before going solo with a string of family dramas and romantic comedies that defined the '80s — Mundhanai Mudichu, Andha 7 Naatkal, Darling, Darling, Darling. He directed over 25 films. He acted in more than 75. He wrote screenplays that studios across the country paid to adapt.

What made him special was the texture. Bhagyaraj never wrote a character who felt like a plot device. His leads were flawed, funny, specific — the kind of people you'd recognize from your own family. His heroines were sharp, not decorative. His comedies had genuine warmth. In an industry that often rewarded spectacle, he built an empire on relatability.

His most recent notable role was in Dhanush's Kuberaa (2025), where he proved at 72 that he could still command a frame. Earlier this year, celebrating his golden jubilee in cinema, he announced plans to return to directing: "From this year onwards, I want to work with renewed enthusiasm."

He never got the chance.

Where It Hurts for the Diaspora

For NRIs who grew up in the '90s, Bhagyaraj's influence is everywhere — even if you never heard his name. Every time you quote a line from *Beta* or remember *Raja Babu* as peak Govinda, you are quoting Bhagyaraj's original Tamil screenplay, filtered through a Hindi dubbing. For Tamil diaspora families, his films *were* the weekend — rented VHS tapes passed between households, the soundtrack of kitchens and living rooms from Edison to Hounslow.

His final rites are scheduled for Sunday at the Besant Nagar crematorium in Chennai, with full state honours. He is survived by his wife Poornima and their two children, Shanthanu and Saranya.

The Screenplay King has left the building. But the scripts — God, the scripts — will keep playing forever.
